title: 2 Chronicles 28:5–15
context: Because of Ahaz’s sin, Syria and Israel defeat Judah, killing many and taking a great number of captives to Samaria. The prophet Oded confronts Israel’s army, and leaders of Ephraim insist the captives be clothed, fed, and returned to Jericho. This account of defeat and mercy appears only in Chronicles; 2 Kings 16:5 says that Rezin and Pekah besieged Ahaz but could not overcome him. The two accounts are named here without harmonization. The scene is largely shared ground about mercy inside judgment.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria. They struck him, and carried away from him a great multitude of captives, and brought them to Damascus. He was also delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with a great slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD delivered Ahaz into the hands of Syria and Israel. Arminian readers see God allowing Judah to suffer the consequences of its king’s choices, and they note that 2 Kings 16:5 says the attackers could not overcome Ahaz.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using the nations as instruments of judgment while remaining just. The Judges 9:23 box discusses how the traditions relate God’s purposes to such agents. The difference from 2 Kings 16:5 is named, not harmonized.

verses.text: For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed in Judah one hundred twenty thousand in one day, all of them valiant men, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Pekah killed one hundred twenty thousand in Judah in one day because they had forsaken the LORD. Arminian readers stress that the people as well as the king had turned away, sharing responsibility for the disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the large number soberly, as interpreters discuss figures like this in different ways. The Chronicler’s explanation is theological: the defeat came because Judah had forsaken the God of their fathers.

verses.text: Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king’s son, Azrikam the ruler of the house, and Elkanah who was next to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Zichri of Ephraim killed the king’s son, the ruler of the house, and the official next to the king. Arminian readers see the cost of Ahaz’s choices reaching into his own household and court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these names appear only in Chronicles. The loss of the king’s son and senior officials shows how close the judgment came to the throne itself.

verses.text: The children of Israel carried away captive of their brothers two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters, and also took away much plunder from them, and brought the plunder to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel took two hundred thousand women and children captive and much plunder to Samaria. Arminian readers note the bitter irony that the captors were their own brothers, children of the same covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the word brothers the tragedy of a divided people. The size of the number, like that in verse 6, is read in different ways by interpreters, but the grief of the scene is plain.

verses.text: But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded; and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria, and said to them, “Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he has delivered them into your hand, and you have slain them in a rage which has reached up to heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet Oded meets the army and says they slew Judah in a rage which has reached up to heaven. Arminian readers see God holding even the instruments of his judgment accountable for cruelty beyond what he intended.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Oded affirms God delivered Judah into Israel’s hand while condemning the excess. God’s use of a nation does not excuse its violence, a principle also seen in Isaiah 10:5-15.

verses.text: Now you intend to degrade the children of Judah and Jerusalem as male and female slaves for yourselves. Aren’t there even with you trespasses of your own against the LORD your God?
verses.arminianNotes: Oded asks, Aren’t there even with you trespasses of your own against the LORD your God? Arminian readers see a call to self-examination, a warning against condemning others while ignoring one’s own sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet exposing Israel’s own guilt. The intent to enslave their brothers would add sin to sin, and the law forbade such treatment of fellow Israelites (Leviticus 25:39-43).

verses.text: Now hear me therefore, and send back the captives that you have taken captive from your brothers, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is on you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Oded commands them to send back the captives, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is on them. Arminian readers see a real opportunity to turn aside further judgment through obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wrath that fell on Judah now threatens Israel. The command to release the captives is both a warning and a mercy, giving the northern kingdom a way to act rightly.

verses.text: Then some of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who came from the war,
verses.arminianNotes: Leaders of Ephraim, named one by one, stand up against the returning army. Arminian readers honor individuals who choose to obey the prophet’s word even against the momentum of victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler records the names of these men, giving lasting honor to their courage. Their response shows that conscience was not dead in the north.

verses.text: and said to them, “You must not bring in the captives here, for you intend that which will bring on us a trespass against the LORD, to add to our sins and to our guilt; for our guilt is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders say that keeping the captives would add to their guilt, for their guilt is great. Arminian readers see genuine conviction leading to action, a model of repentance that changes behavior.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in their confession, our guilt is great, a rare moment of national self-awareness. They recognize that sin accumulates and that God’s patience should not be presumed upon.

verses.text: So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the princes and all the assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: The armed men leave the captives and the plunder before the princes and the assembly. Arminian readers note that soldiers flush with victory chose to let go of their gain, a costly act of obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the whole assembly witnesses the release. The scene shows that God’s word, brought by a prophet, could still turn a people from a wrong course.

verses.text: The men who have been mentioned by name rose up and took the captives, and with the plunder clothed all who were naked among them, dressed them, gave them sandals, gave them something to eat and to drink, anointed them, carried all the feeble of them on donkeys, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: The captives are clothed, fed, anointed, the feeble carried on donkeys, and brought to Jericho. Many readers hear an echo of this scene in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37), and Arminian readers see compassion shown to enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see mercy shown within a time of judgment, as Israelites care for their wounded brothers from Judah. The detailed kindness stands in contrast to the cruelty of the battle described just before.
